description: KhetSat turns NASA climate and soil data into simple, district-level guidance that helps farmers in Andhra Pradesh adapt their crops, sowing dates and water use to a changing climate. Over the hackathon weekend we’ll build a working app with a risk map, crop and sowing suggestions, and plain-language advice in Telugu, Hindi and English.
summary:
A rain-fed farmer must choose a crop before knowing how the monsoon will go. In Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh, monsoon rain has ranged from 144 mm to 611 mm since 1981.

KhetSat is a free web app that answers one question before sowing: which crop rotation holds up when the rains don't? For a place, it takes the rotation grown today and two alternatives, replays each one day by day through 45 years of NASA POWER weather data, and checks whether each crop got the water it needed. It then says the result in plain words, reads it aloud, and takes questions by voice, in English and six Indian languages, so farmers who do not read can use it.

It works for three pre-analysed districts and for any other point in India, with the farmer's own soil. Every answer is built from the computed numbers, never written by a language model. The seasons it marks as failed in Anantapur match reported drought years, and the ranking of rotations is unchanged when the analysis is repeated with GPM IMERG satellite rainfall. Limits are stated in the app: figures describe a 50 km grid cell, and prices and yields are not counted.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

KhetSat compares crop rotations for a place using 45 years of NASA weather data. For each rotation it shows why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, what is not known, and what to check locally. The first screen gives the result in everyday words with one large "Hear the result" button.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Daily rain and temperature for 1981 to 2025 come from the NASA POWER API for the chosen point.

2. A crop water balance (FAO-56 method) runs each rotation day by day through every year and scores each season by the share of the crop's water need that was met. Below 50% counts as a failed season.

3. The farmer sets five priorities with sliders (a normal year, a poor year, using less water, building the soil, breaking pest cycles) and the ranking updates.

4. The farmer can set their soil by type, from the SoilGrids map, or by typing a known value; the 45 years are re-run with it.

5. A map shows NASA GIBS satellite layers (MODIS vegetation, SMAP soil moisture, VIIRS true colour) by month and year.

6. A voice guide answers eight common questions by tap, typing or speech, and reads answers aloud in seven languages.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- A farmer hears, before sowing, how each choice fared in dry years, in their own language.

- In Anantapur, alternating groundnut with millet needs 14% less crop water than groundnut every year and adds a second crop family.

- It also shows when an alternative is worse: millet followed by chickpea failed in 20 of 44 seasons.

- It works for any point in India, not only the three pre-analysed districts.

KhetSat supports a decision. It does not replace the farmer's judgment or the local agriculture officer.

HOW ACCURATE IT IS

- The five seasons marked as failed for groundnut in Anantapur (2002, 2003, 2016, 2018, 2023) are all reported drought years. The check runs one way: milder declared droughts show as below-normal seasons, not failures.

- Repeating the analysis with GPM IMERG satellite rainfall (2001 to 2025) leaves the ranking of rotations unchanged at all three locations.

- NASA POWER rainfall in Anantapur is roughly 9% to 14% above published rain-gauge normals.

- 37 unit tests cover the calculations; the in-browser engine matches the Python pipeline on 546 compared values.

- Voice guide: on 120 natural phrasings in English, Telugu and Hindi, keyword matching routed 53% correctly and the AI question router 97%. All 12 out-of-scope questions were declined.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (standard library only) for the data pipeline; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the app, with no build step; Leaflet for the map; the browser's Web Speech API for listening and speaking; a Cloudflare Worker calling a Claude model as an optional question router; GitHub Pages for hosting.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- The answer is spoken, in plain words, without charts or percentages, for people who do not read.

- The AI model only names which question was asked. It never sees the data and never writes an answer, so the guide cannot say anything the numbers do not support.

- Every result carries its own limits: what is not known, and what to check locally.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Low literacy, seven languages, phones with slow connections (a static site), honesty about uncertainty, and open, published methods.

NOT YET DONE

Field soil tests, prices and yields, a statistical comparison with yield records, and native-speaker review of the translations.

LINKS

Live app: https://demonjd2026-afk.github.io/khetsat/

Full demo video (4:53): https://youtu.be/NaSWAxlDzoc

Methods: https://github.com/demonjd2026-afk/khetsat/blob/main/docs/METHODS.md

USE OF AI

Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding and drafting assistant for the code and documentation, and to draft and machine-review the translations. The app's optional question router calls a Claude model. The voices in the demo video are AI-generated (Piper text-to-speech). The crop and water calculations use no AI.
